Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major. Widely known as the Eroica, Ludwig van Beethoven's Symphony No. 3, Op. 55, completed in 1804, stands as one of the most pivotal works in music history. It marks the boundary between the Classical and Romantic eras, running twice as long as previous symphonies and far more emotionally intense.

Beethoven originally dedicated the symphony to Napoleon Bonaparte, whom he admired as a hero of the French Revolution's democratic ideals. But when he heard that Napoleon had crowned himself Emperor of the French, Beethoven flew into a rage and scratched out the dedication on the title page so violently that he tore the paper. When published, the work was retitled Sinfonia Eroica, or Heroic Symphony, and was instead dedicated to celebrate the memory of a great man.

The first movement opens with two abrupt, fortissimo chords in E-flat major, followed by a cello-led main theme that unexpectedly dips to a chromatic C-sharp, creating harmonic tension. During the transition to the recapitulation, the horn enters with the main theme four measures before the rest of the orchestra, a famous moment known as the horn false entry. The story goes that Beethoven's pupil Ferdinand Ries mistakenly criticized the horn player for miscounting.

The second movement is a solemn, tragic funeral march in C minor, featuring a sobbing oboe melody and a dramatic fugal section. The third movement is a rapid, energetic scherzo with a trio featuring three French horns playing hunting calls. The fourth movement and finale is based on a melody from Beethoven's own 1801 ballet The Creatures of Prometheus. The movement exposes only the bass line of the theme first before building the full melody.

Eroica marked a radical departure from the chamber-like symmetry of Haydn and Mozart, introducing a massive development section and a programmatic narrative of heroic struggle, death, and rebirth. It was first performed publicly at the Theater an der Wien in 1805. The funeral march later became famous in its own right, performed at the memorial ceremonies of many public figures, including the state funeral of Felix Mendelssohn, and was broadcast by German radio to announce the defeat at the Battle of Stalingrad. The work initiated Beethoven's middle heroic period and effectively launched the Romantic era in symphonic music.
